#9020. Are seed oils bad for you? Vegetable oil vs. olive oil vs. butter

From TikTok to bestseller lists, vegetable oils—a.k.a. “seed oils”—are a big topic right now.

To be fair, folks have debated the merits of vegetable oils dating back to when they first entered the marketplace.

More recently, however, with the advent of the carnivore diet, vegetable oil hate has roared back into the socials. Maybe you’ve come across posts that refer to these cooking oils as “toxic sludge,” “motor oil,” “the hateful eight,” and “the biggest cause of chronic disease that nobody knows about.”

The anti-vegetable oil logic goes something like this…

Animal fats have been with humans for thousands of years. Vegetable fats, on the other hand, were invented during the last century when profit-seeking companies wanted to find a way to sell cheap-to-grow foods to unsuspecting consumers.

Another argument: Like margarine, vegetable oils were marketed as healthier alternatives for butter, and yet, people argue, these oils are worse than butter, raising your risk for obesity, anxiety, depression, ulcerative colitis, and more.

In contrast to the above line of thought, other experts will tell you that vegetable oils are harmless, potentially even health-promoting—and absolutely better than butter.

Like so many nutrition topics, the truth is too nuanced to fit on a meme.

In this story, we’ll help you sort the science from the pseudoscience so you can make informed decisions about the oils you choose to include in your diet.

Sometimes called “seed oils,” vegetable oils start, as you might suspect, from the seed of a plant. The most common ones you’ll find in a typical grocery aisle include:

By the way, if you feel like there’s a bunch of oils missing from that list, it’s probably because those oils come from non-seed plants (such as olive, avocado, palm, or coconut oil, which all come from fruits, and aren’t considered vegetable or seed oils).

Non-vegetable oils—such as olive and avocado oil—are derived from naturally fatty foods. In fact, olives are so oily that you could theoretically make your own olive oil at home. (Just Google “how to make olive oil from scratch,” and you’ll find a number of videos walking you through the steps.)

The same can’t be said of most vegetable oils, which mostly come from foods with a relatively tiny fat content to begin with.

Case in point: A cup of green olives contains about 20 grams of fat,1 whereas a cup of corn has 2 grams.2

As a result, manufacturers must use an extensive multi-step process to extract this small amount of oil from these non-oily foods. These steps include:

During this process, health-promoting polyphenols and other stabilizing nutrients are lost, and small amounts of unsaturated fats are transformed into trans fatty acids (also called partially hydrogenated fat).

(Interesting fact: This also happens during deep frying. When vegetable oils sizzle in a restaurant’s deep fryer for hours, the trans fat content of the oil increases.)

To call these processed oils “toxic” might be an exaggeration. However, nutrition scientists generally agree that people should avoid trans fats in the diet, and in 2018, the Food and Drug Administration banned manufacturers from adding trans fats to processed foods.3 4

At PN, we’ve created several visual guides people can use to make informed decisions about what to eat.

(We’ve also created a shopping list, which you or your clients can print out and take to the grocery store. Check it out: Healthy Fats Shopping List)

In these guides, we’ve placed a few vegetable oils—expeller-pressed canola oil, high-oleic sunflower, and safflower oils—in the “Eat Some” section. For us, “eat some” is another way of saying that these foods will neither improve health nor harm health—when consumed in reasonable amounts. In some cases, like in the example of dark chocolate, when consumed in small amounts, they might even improve health.

The rest of the vegetable oils, along with butter and other saturated fats, fall into the “Eat Less” category, as the image below shows. You’ll find vegetable oils in bold.

We’ve gotten hate mail from folks who say certain vegetable oils—especially cold-pressed canola oil—should appear alongside olive oil in the “eat more” category. Plenty of others say all vegetable oils belong in the “eat less” column, and that butter belongs in “eat some” or even “eat more.”

To understand the scientific reasoning behind our recommendations, let’s explore some head-to-head matchups.

These oils are the least refined of their kind.

To make extra virgin olive oil (EVOO), manufacturers grind and mechanically press olives, without using any heat. Similarly, expeller-pressed canola oil is made by mechanically pressing rapeseed, without the use of heat or chemical solvents.

Olive oil is richer in heart-healthy monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) than almost any other cooking oil.

In addition, unlike the more refined “light” olive oil, EVOO maintains most of the olive fruit’s original polyphenols. These plant-based substances help to combat inflammation and protect cells from damage.

More studies vouch for EVOO’s health-promoting qualities than for any other cooking fat.

For example, researchers asked 22,892 adults from Southern Italy to self-report their olive oil consumption. People who consumed the most olive oil (more than two tablespoons a day) were 20 percent less likely to die over the 13-year study than people who consumed the least olive oil (less than one tablespoon a day).5

Other research has linked the consumption of olive oil with a reduced risk of:

Consumption of olive oil is also associated with reductions in LDL cholesterol, especially when used to replace saturated fats like butter and coconut oil.10

Years ago, culinary experts recommended using EVOO only on salads and other uncooked foods. Back then, they assumed EVOO’s relatively low smoke point (350 to 410F) meant the oil would break down when heated, losing some of its distinctive flavor and health benefits.

We now know that smoke point isn’t as big a deal as previously thought.

That’s especially true in the case of EVOO, whose polyphenols and high concentrations of monounsaturated fats help keep the oil stable when heated.

In research that heated a variety of cooking oils to 464 F (240C) and then held them at 356 F (180C) for several hours, EVOO remained more stable than any other oil tested, including canola oil.11

One of the more affordable cooking oils on the shelf, canola oil, is made from a Canadian-made hybrid of the rapeseed plant.

(The word “canola” refers to the first three letters of “Canada” with a fun “ola” added to the end for marketing purposes.)12

Among vegetable oils, canola is the richest in heart-healthy monounsaturated fats (though several non-vegetable oils have it beat) as well as alpha-linolenic acid, a plant-based omega-3 fatty acid.

In addition, canola oil contains plant substances called phytosterols that help influence blood cholesterol for the better, especially when used as a substitute for butter, research has found.13 14 15

Extra virgin olive oil is the clear winner.

The body of research in support of EVOO dwarfs the body of research in support of expeller-pressed canola.

In addition, EVOO has a more favorable fatty acid profile. By the way, so does avocado oil, which is why you’ll also find it in the “eat more” column.

However, you can buy roughly twice as much expeller-pressed canola oil for half as much money as EVOO. Because of this, expeller-pressed canola can be a good budget-friendly choice. In addition, because of expeller-pressed canola’s more neutral flavor, many people prefer it over EVOO for baking.

When used in moderation, expeller-pressed canola can be part of a healthy diet. It is likely to be at least health neutral, if not somewhat health beneficial.

This match-up comes down to how processing methods affect the end product.

An expeller press is a machine that squeezes oil out of seeds.

It’s able to do this without the use of solvents or heat, which helps preserve beneficial compounds such as alpha-linolenic acid and phytosterols.

Refining removes some protective alpha-linoleic acid while adding small amounts of unhealthy trans fatty acids. This results in a product that is proportionally lower in omega-3 fatty acids and higher in omega-6 fatty acids.

Expeller-pressed canola oil wins, but only by a small margin.

That’s because canola oil starts with a less controversial fatty acid profile than many other vegetable oils, as the chart below shows. Soybean oil, for example, has less heart-healthy monounsaturated fat and much more theoretically inflammation-contributing omega-6 fat.

The typical American consumes around 16 to 20 times more omega-6 fats than omega-3s.

This imbalance could theoretically increase inflammation in your body, potentially raising your risk for diabetes, obesity, and other health problems, argue some experts.16

Years ago, the recommendation to balance your omega 6s with omega 3s was widespread. (The suggested “ideal” ratio: Anywhere from 1:1 to 4:1, in favor of omega 6s.)

These days, there’s more debate among nutritional scientists as to whether this imbalance contributes to chronic inflammation, especially when those omega 6s are consumed in whole foods that contain many other beneficial compounds.

For example, nuts and seeds—both naturally rich in omega-6 fats—have been associated with a range of health benefits, including reductions in blood cholesterol and inflammation.17 18

In 2019, Harvard Health ran the headline “No need to avoid healthy omega-6 fats.” In support of their argument, a 2019 study from the American Heart Association journal Circulation determined that, if anything, the consumption of omega-6 fats reduced the risk for stroke, heart disease, and early death.19

However, while nuts and refined canola oil may share a somewhat similar fatty acid profile, the two foods differ in one important way. As we mentioned earlier, refined canola oil is basically pure oil. Meanwhile, nuts and seeds come packaged with health-protective fiber, polyphenols, protein, vitamins, and minerals.

Minimally-processed foods, like nuts or extra virgin oils, include a complex matrix of health-promoting nutrients. Highly-processed oils, on the other hand, have lost the vast majority of those healthful compounds, leaving mostly just the fatty acids which are more prone to oxidation (we’ll cover that next).

This is the match-up that triggers the most arguing on the interwebs.

Let’s cover the major claims from both sides—plus what the research says.

Butter proponents argue that saturated fats have been unnecessarily vilified. They point to nutrition recommendations during the 1980s and 1990s that recommended people replace butter with trans-fat rich margarine.

Margarine aside, others claim the research in support of reducing saturated fats is thin at best.20

However, excessive saturated fat consumption (beyond 10 percent of total calories) does seem to boost cholesterol levels and may increase your risk of heart disease.21

Some research has found that replacing 5 percent of the saturated fats in your diet with monounsaturated fats could reduce the risk of heart disease by 15 percent. Similarly, replacing 5 percent of the saturated fats in your diet with polyunsaturated fats (with most of that coming from refined vegetable oils) reduces the risk of a future heart attack by 10 percent, according to an analysis of eight studies involving 13,614 people.22 Many other studies support this finding.23

But not all saturated fats affect blood cholesterol equally. In some dairy foods, a membrane—called a milk fat globule membrane—surrounds the saturated fats and seems to limit their cholesterol-raising properties.

However, butter is low in this protective membrane, and consequently raises blood cholesterol more than other high-fat dairy products, like full-fat milk, cream, yogurt, or cheese.24 25 26

The U.S. Dietary Guidelines recommend capping saturated fat at less than 10 percent of your calorie intake. A tablespoon of butter contains 7 grams of saturated fat—a third of the recommended daily limit in a 2000 Calorie diet.

So, while you don’t necessarily need to eliminate butter, it’s worth moderating your intake.

(Interested in learning about all the nuances of saturated fat consumption? Read: Is saturated fat good or bad for you?)

Due to their chemical structure, polyunsaturated fats are inherently less stable and more prone to oxidation than saturated or monounsaturated fats.

During the refining process, protective phytochemicals and antioxidants are stripped, making these oils more prone to oxidation. The theory is that this oxidation increases inflammation in the body and elevates the risk of various health conditions.

There’s some evidence to suggest that diets rich in polyunsaturated fats, especially from refined vegetable oils, are associated with increased levels of oxidized blood lipids, lipid peroxidation, and other markers of inflammation.27 28

If you only use refined corn or safflower oils to lightly coat veggies before roasting them, you likely don’t have much to worry about.

However, for the vast majority of people, the biggest source of refined vegetable oils isn’t home-cooked meals—it’s ultra-processed foods.

The extra processing and repeated heat exposure used to create ultra-processed foods further oxidize these oils. Additionally, these foods are often loaded with potentially harmful ingredients like added sodium and sugars, and low in beneficial nutrients like fiber, vitamins, minerals, and phytonutrients.

Plus, they’re incredibly calorie-dense and difficult to stop eating, which can raise your risk for obesity. (Find out exactly why highly-processed foods are so “addictive”: Why you can’t stop eating ultra-processed foods.)

In a large review involving nearly 10 million people, the consumption of ultra-processed foods was associated with a higher risk of premature death.29 In addition, studies have linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods with the following health problems:30 31 32 33

You don’t have to abolish ultra-processed foods.

But your health will benefit from capping your consumption to about 20 percent or so of your intake, with the other 80 percent or so from mostly minimally-processed whole foods.

This alone will naturally lower your refined vegetable oil intake to a safer level, without much fuss. Plus, consuming refined vegetable oils in the context of a diet that’s rich in colorful plants, fiber, phytochemicals, and antioxidants may help offset the concern of oxidation. (For example, by putting a reasonable amount of commercial salad dressing on a large, colorful salad.)

Ultimately, both should be limited in the diet, and neither are health-promoting.

Most refined vegetable oils are lopsidedly rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids compared to monounsaturated fats, and are stripped of many protective compounds. As mentioned earlier, some experts argue that these omega-6-rich fats may contribute to inflammation (but the evidence here is mixed). Because of how they’re processed, seed oils also contain some of those trans fats that everyone agrees we should all minimize.

In contrast, butter is low in omega 6s but high in saturated fat, which can be problematic in higher amounts. Especially since it’s so low in the protective milk fat globule membrane. However, compared to refined vegetable oil, butter is less processed. Like olive oil, it’s one of those fats you could theoretically make at home.

This might be obvious from the head-to-head matchups, but we’ll say it anyway.

If you like it and can afford it, EVOO is a great choice.

Cold-pressed avocado oil and walnut oil are also great options, as both are rich in antioxidant compounds. Like EVOO, avocado oil is a rich source of MUFAs. Walnut oil’s fat primarily comes from polyunsaturated fats, so it’s best used as a dressing rather than used for cooking (as it’s less heat stable).

However, like EVOO, avocado and walnut oil tend to be expensive. If you or your client are budget-conscious, expeller-pressed canola oil is a solid runner-up.

Similarly, high-oleic sunflower and safflower oils are richer sources of monounsaturated fats than their high-linoleic cousins. When substituted for saturated fats like butter, high-oleic oils have been associated with cardiovascular benefits.34 35

Regardless of what cooking fats you or your client choose, you’ll also want to do the following:

Whole and minimally-processed foods—such as nuts, seeds, avocados, olives, and salmon—are more likely to feature health-promoting monounsaturated (MUFAs) and omega-3 fats. They also come packaged with a wide array of other good-for-you nutrients such as fiber, protein, minerals, and antioxidants.

In contrast, ultra-professed foods are generally devoid of everything you keep hearing you should consume more of. These foods also tend to be calorie-dense, highly rewarding, and hard to stop eating.

If you’re not sure whether packaged food is minimally processed or highly processed, take a close look and consider:

If you answer “no” to most of the above, the food is likely highly processed.

It doesn’t matter what source of fat is used to fry them.

Sort all fried foods into the “eat less” category.

EVOO is associated with longer, healthier lives. However, that doesn’t mean you should be doing shots of it.

As a general rule, you’re better off getting most of your fat from foods like avocados, olives, nuts and seeds than from any cooking oil.

Whole food fats are rich in fiber, phytochemicals, vitamins, and minerals, and are generally less calorie-dense than oils. (But having one to three servings of oils or butter per day is reasonable.)

And if you want personalized advice to suit your body, your eating preferences, and your goals, check out our Nutrition Calculator to figure out how fats fit into your overall diet.

#9019. What Really Happened When the Men and Women Raced Kona Together Again

Triathlete contributor Jordan Blanco interviewed female Kona fans and age-group women over the course of a week she spent on the Big Island leading up to covering the Ironman World Championship. Blanco has attended 12 Ironman World Championship events (11 Kona, one Nice) and raced it nine times (eight Kona, one St. George).

If the 2026 Ironman World Championship delivered one thing, it was drama.

Vincent Luis (FRA) became the Ironman world champion on his Kona debut but also in the final race of his career. It was a mic drop moment for the three-time Olympian. Taylor Knibb (USA) finally claimed the title that eluded her in 2025, following one of the most exciting finishes in the history of the women’s race. Defending champion Solveig Løvseth (NOR) appeared to be heading for a second consecutive victory before collapsing in the final kilometer, allowing Knibb to reclaim the lead and take the win.

This kind of racing makes Kona special. Unpredictable, unforgiving, and compelling viewing until the very end.

But beyond the professional racing, this year’s world championship marked another milestone: For the first time since 2019, men and women competed together on the Big Island on the same day.

After three years of separate men’s and women’s championships, Ironman committed to bringing everyone back together. The decision was broadly welcomed by athletes. Couples could race together again, and the sport’s biggest names were back to sharing the same stage.

However, women, specifically, had legitimate concerns about what might be lost in the process. Would the professional women receive the same coverage as the men? Would age-group women have a fair race on a more congested course? And could Kona accommodate everyone.

As we wrap up coverage of the race, here’s what appeared to work, what didn’t and what Ironman might want to consider — from the women’s perspective — before October 2027.

Let’s start with the positives. The professional races were exceptional, and the decision to separate the men’s and women’s races by 10 minutes worked well in preserving the integrity of both competitions. With age-group athletes starting later, there was little interference with the professional fields.

Ironman also made a genuine effort to address one of the longstanding criticisms of single-day racing: the tendency for the men’s racing to dominate the main broadcast. Ironman CEO Scott DeRue had committed to equal coverage of the men’s and women’s races. The broadcast production included multiple feeds, including a “quad box” allowing fans to follow different cameras alongside the main broadcast.

Alison Freeman, a longtime triathlon coach who watched from Colorado, with a group of athletes, was pleasantly surprised.

“I remember thinking at some point, maybe the second half of the bike, that they had done and were doing a very good job of providing balanced coverage between the men’s and women’s races,” Freeman says. “I didn’t feel like we were watching the men’s race and occasionally cutting over to the women’s race.”

For much of the day, the broadcast appeared to deliver on DeRue’s promise. That was until the leading men approached the finish line. Freeman had gone into the championship concerned that the men’s finish would coincide with a critical stage of the women’s marathon, as had happened during prior combined championships.

That is precisely when the coverage began to unravel. As the top 10 men crossed the finish line, the women’s “race ticker” disappeared from the main broadcast. Meanwhile the supplementary feeds that Freeman had been relying on began to malfunction. One went black, and another froze on footage of Knibb. For approximately 10 minutes, Freeman and her guests had virtually no reliable information on the status of the women’s race. They turned to the Ironman tracking app, but the information there was also inconsistent.

“We couldn’t see what was going on with her,” Freeman recalls of Knibb. “So it was basically this 10-minute essentially blackout on the top two women in the race with no data, no visuals.”

Fortunately, coverage returned before Løvseth made her pass on Knibb and viewers witnessed that key moment. But Freeman argues that whether the broadcast missed a critical pass is beside the point.

“To me, equal coverage is … do I get an equal sense of what is going on in both races?” she explains. “An equal understanding of the moves, the passes, who’s faltering, who’s looking strong.”

Triathlete’s own internal analysis found that approximately 56.5% of the broadcast was devoted to the men compared with 41.6% for the women, with the remainder consisting of scenery and other miscellaneous footage. The analysis also found that helicopter footage during the bike leg was almost exclusively focused on the men’s race. The notable exception being when the leading men passed by the leading women going in the opposite direction.

Producing race coverage for two simultaneous races is a difficult undertaking, particularly when decisive moments overlap. However, Ironman demonstrated throughout the day that split screen coverage was possible. Why then did the women’s race coverage disappear from the main broadcast when it mattered most?

Freeman sees a straightforward solution: Keep both races visible, even when the attention shifts to the men’s finish.

“If you want women to be in the sport, you should show women being in the sport, right?” she says.

While the professionals enjoyed largely separate races, the age-group athletes had a very different experience. Ironman’s wave-start schedule was designed to manage thousands of swimmers entering Kailua Bay, with age groups alternating between women and men rather than separating genders entirely.

If we’re looking at the women’s experience exclusively, the oldest women started first at 6:38 a.m., followed by older men. The younger men’s age groups began at 7:05 a.m., with women aged 40-54 starting at 7:25 a.m. The men’s 45-49 and 50-54 groups followed, before the youngest women finally entered the water at 7:40 a.m., followed by men aged 55-59 at 7:45 a.m.

For strong swimmers among the younger women, the consequences were significant. Victoria Feng, who finished eighth in the women’s 25-29 age group, described an extraordinarily difficult swim.

Feng was among the fastest female age-group swimmers, but starting behind slower male swimmers, she quickly encountered significant traffic. She estimates that she had clear water for only about five minutes before catching the waves ahead. The data bears it out; given her 56:55 swim split, Feng outswam 233 of the eventual 240 finishers in the men’s 55-59 age group by more than five minutes — though it’s also worth noting that Feng’s experience is an exceptional outlier.

She describes men grabbing, kicking, and pulling at her shoulders as she attempted to pass. Around the turnaround boat, she describes swimmers breaststroking directly in her path, forcing her toward the boat. The final approach to the pier was no better, with congestion in the narrow swim chute, making it difficult to navigate safely.

“This is not a way to run a world championship where women are significantly disadvantaged straight from the start,” she says.

Not every woman experienced the same problems, however.

Jana Richtrova, who finished second in the women’s 45-49 age group, reported a relatively uneventful swim despite the challenging ocean conditions. Richtrova started at 7:25 a.m. and swam approximately 1:15, a performance she was delighted with given the choppy water.

“Swim was completely fine,” she reports. “There was no aggression.”

She even attempted to jump on the feet of faster men as they came through from behind. But Richtrova still questions the decision to intersperse the women’s waves among the men’s, noting the previous combined championships had provided greater separation to provide fairer racing. Starting all the women behind the men might mean later starts, with greater exposure to heat and wind, but she believes it would produce a more equitable racing environment.

The contrasting experiences illustrate the complexity of designing wave starts for a combined championship. What works for a 1:15 swimmer may be considerably more successful than for someone swimming sub-1 hour.

While the swim created problems for Feng and some fellow competitors but not others, Feng and Richtrovra report similar experiences on the bike course.

Both Feng and Richtrova describe extensive drafting, crowded roads, and difficulty maintaining legal separation from other riders.

“I wish I was exaggerating when I said it was like the Tour de France out there,” Feng says.

She reports repeatedly encountering packs of 15 to 20 age-group athletes riding together.

“For the first 30 miles, it was pretty much impossible to ride legally most of the time,” she says.

Instead of riding at her planned power, she found herself deciding whether to surge past groups of athletes or drop well below race effort to reestablish legal spacing.

Richtrova had similar complaints. Shortly after leaving T1, she witnessed three men riding wheel to wheel on Kuakini Highway. As they approached the turnaround, the third rider touched the wheel of a rider ahead and crashed. On the Queen Ka’ahumanu Highway, she described large groups of athletes riding together, leaving limited space for athletes to pass safely. Even when Richtrova deliberately opened a legal gap, she experienced athletes cutting in dangerously close to her front wheel.

Neither woman knows exactly how the drafting affected results. Richtrova acknowledged that even riders making a genuine effort to follow the rules benefit from the presence of others.

However, the extent of the congestion raises questions about whether enough was done to enforce fair racing. Feng says she didn’t see a single referee and observed only one athlete in a penalty tent during the race. This of course contrasts with the pro event, which saw extensive penalty enforcement that had major implications to both genders’ podiums.

One of the less obvious consequences for women of returning to a combined race was the new combined transition tent. Richtrova, a veteran of multiple Kona championships, was surprised to discover that the traditional separate men’s and women’s change tents were now a single, shared tent. Private areas were available for athletes needing to change clothes, but the main changing area was mixed gender. For Richtrova, accustomed to a relatively quiet women’s transition tent, the experience was considerably more chaotic.

“It was just like, we’re here with the guys, and there’s a couple of us, and the rest is just men,” she recalls.

She praised the volunteers who continued to provide excellent assistance but questioned whether the new arrangements had been communicated clearly enough. A fellow competitor, she says, was initially directed into the men’s private changing area before discovering where she was supposed to go.

In many respects, yes. The professional races delivered unforgettable drama. The logistics of bringing both genders together appeared manageable. And it was special to see men and women sharing the Kona stage again.

But the combined event also exposed some weaknesses from the women’s perspective. Ironman made progress with its broadcast, only to lose sight (literally) of the women during one of its most important stretches. The wave start structure created very different swimming experiences for age-group women, while bike-course congestion and drafting raises questions about the fairness of the competition.

Ironman has a year to rethink the wave starts, review its drafting enforcement for age-groupers, improve communication around transition arrangements, and ensure its broadcast can follow two professional races simultaneously without sacrificing either one.

The most accessible, repeatable high-value hotel redemption in travel rewards

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: You've been grinding toward your FI number, optimizing every dollar, and you've accumulated a stash of Chase Ultimate Rewards points sitting in your account. Now imagine checking into a clean, comfortable Hyatt Place in a city you're visiting for a wedding, a family reunion, or a long weekend — and the front desk agent hands you your keycard while your account balance drops by exactly 5,000 points. Not $150. Not $180. Five thousand points that you earned by buying groceries. That's the Category 1 Hyatt sweet spot — and it's the single most accessible, repeatable, high-value redemption in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A standard night at a Hyatt Place or Hyatt House in a mid-size U.S. city routinely runs **$100–$200 per night** in cash. At 5,000 points per night, you're redeeming at **2–4 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that demolishes the standard 1 cent per point benchmark that most casual rewards users never surpass. At 4 CPP on a $200 night, you're getting four times the value of a simple cash-back card. Every. Single. Time. The pricing inefficiency here is structural, not accidental. World of Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** — meaning a Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in January or a Friday night during a sold-out college football weekend when cash rates are spiking. The loyalty program doesn't dynamically price awards the way airlines do. That fixed ceiling is your edge. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption isn't just good — it's foundational. It's the first sweet spot that proves the system works. Before you're ready to redeem 60,000 points for a business class flight to Tokyo, you need to feel what it's like to hand over a handful of points and walk into a hotel room that would have cost you real money. This is that moment. It builds the muscle memory, the confidence, and the conviction that travel rewards are real — and that you're playing the game correctly. This is where the journey starts.

World of Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value of any major hotel loyalty program. While Hilton and Marriott have moved to dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate based on demand — Hyatt maintains a fixed award chart. This structural difference is your edge. A Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it is a quiet Tuesday in February or a sold-out homecoming weekend. Combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer ratios (1:1 from Sapphire Reserve, 4:3 from Sapphire Preferred) and instant transfer speed, Hyatt redemptions are the single best use of UR points for hotel stays. The ChooseFI community considers this the entry point that proves the entire travel rewards system works.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

The core insight behind this sweet spot is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt uses a fixed-price award chart, and Category 1 is priced at a floor that hasn't kept pace with rising hotel cash rates.

Most hotel loyalty programs have moved to dynamic pricing — meaning award nights fluctuate with demand, just like cash rates. Marriott Bonvoy, Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards — they've all largely eliminated fixed charts in favor of algorithms that squeeze more points out of you when demand is high. Hyatt has held the line on a fixed chart, and that stubbornness is your opportunity.

The Category 1 floor sits at 5,000 points per night. As cash rates for qualifying properties have climbed with inflation — many now regularly pricing at $150–$200+ — the points cost has remained anchored. The gap between what the market charges and what Hyatt charges in points is widening in your favor every year. That's not a bug in the system. It's a feature you're uniquely positioned to exploit by understanding it.

This redemption is built on two of the best transferable points currencies available to everyday consumers:

Both transfers are instant, which means you can search for availability before committing your points, confirm the room you want is bookable, and then initiate the transfer and complete the booking — all in one sitting. This is a critical distinction from some airline partners where transfers take 24–72 hours and you're transferring on faith. With Hyatt, there's no leap of faith required.

The transfer ratio matters. With a Sapphire Reserve, every UR point becomes one Hyatt point — 15,000 UR points covers three Category 1 nights with zero waste. With a Sapphire Preferred, the 4:3 ratio means you need 20,000 UR points for the same 15,000 Hyatt points. Bilt transfers at 1:1.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award bookings. This matters more for higher-tier redemptions, but it's worth internalizing as a feature of the program overall. When you book 5,000 points for a hotel night, that's your cost. You'll pay any applicable taxes at checkout — typically $10–$25 — but there are no program-imposed carrier fees or redemption surcharges eating into your value.

Hyatt's full chart runs from 3,500 points (Category 1 standard) up to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. Understanding this structure helps you see the Category 1 sweet spot in context: it's the entry point, but it's not a consolation prize. Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties are upper-midscale hotels — clean, well-maintained, often with free breakfast at Hyatt House locations and complimentary parking in suburban markets. These aren't budget motels. You're getting a genuinely comfortable night's sleep for points that most people have already earned without trying.

Booking a Category 1 Hyatt award is one of the smoothest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's exactly how to do it from start to finish.

Before anything else, log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards or your Bilt Rewards account at biltrewards.com and confirm your current points balance. You need a minimum of 5,000 points per night to execute this redemption. If you have 15,000 points, you can book up to three nights.

Go to hyatt.com and log in or create a free World of Hyatt account (it's free to join). Use the search bar to enter your destination city and travel dates. Once results populate, filter by "Points" or "Use Points" using the toggle at the top of the results page. This will display the award rate alongside the cash rate for every property.

Filter further by selecting "Category 1–2" under the Points filter to quickly surface the lowest-cost options. Availability is typically strong — Hyatt.com shows real-time award inventory, and Category 1 properties almost always have rooms open. The booking window extends 395 days out, so you can plan well in advance for travel around a specific event.

Once you've found the property and dates you want, note the exact points cost displayed. For Category 1 properties, this should read 5,000 points per night. Add the room to your cart and proceed — but do not check out yet if your Hyatt account currently has zero balance.

Open a new browser tab and navigate to your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards) or Bilt dashboard. Select "Transfer to Travel Partners" and choose World of Hyatt from the list. Enter the number of points you need (5,000 per night, minimum), confirm your World of Hyatt membership number, and initiate the transfer.

Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant. Note: Sapphire Reserve transfers at 1:1 while Sapphire Preferred transfers at 4:3 (4 UR = 3 Hyatt). Refresh your Hyatt account and your points will be there, ready to use.

Return to your Hyatt browser tab and complete the checkout process. Select "Redeem Points" as your payment method, confirm the points deduction matches what you expected, and finalize the reservation. You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

If your preferred property shows no award availability on your dates, try these workarounds:

Always verify that your desired dates show award availability before initiating a transfer from Chase or Bilt. While transfers are instant, confirming availability first ensures you never have orphaned points sitting in your Hyatt account with no immediate use.

Log into your Chase or Bilt account, navigate to the transfer partners section, select World of Hyatt, and transfer the exact number of points needed. Transfers are instant. With a Sapphire Reserve, 5,000 UR points become 5,000 Hyatt points (1:1). With a Sapphire Preferred, you need approximately 6,700 UR points for 5,000 Hyatt points (4:3 ratio). Bilt transfers at 1:1.

Once the points land in your Hyatt account, complete the booking through hyatt.com or the World of Hyatt app. You will pay applicable taxes at checkout (typically $10 to $25 per night) but no additional redemption fees.

Before booking, note the cash rate for the same room and dates. Divide the cash rate by 5,000 to calculate your cents per point. If a room costs $150 per night and you are paying 5,000 points, you are getting 3 cents per point — triple the baseline 1 cent per point cash back value.

Let's make this concrete. You're flying into Nashville for a long weekend — maybe it's a bachelorette party, a music festival, or just a trip you've been putting off. You pull up Hyatt.com and search Nashville for a Friday–Sunday stay (two nights).

The Hyatt Place Nashville / Brentwood shows cash rates of $169 per night — that's $338 for your two-night stay before taxes. Totally reasonable for Nashville on a weekend, but $338 is $338.

Now look at the award column: 5,000 points per night. Two nights: 10,000 points.

You transferred 10,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points from your Sapphire Reserve to World of Hyatt last week (it took about 30 seconds, and at 1:1 every point landed). Your Hyatt account shows a 10,000-point balance. You complete the booking, pay the ~$30 in taxes at checkout, and you're done.

That's more than three times the value most people extract from their points programs. And those 10,000 Chase UR points? You earned them by putting your regular monthly spending on your Chase Sapphire card for a few months.

At the Hyatt Place, you'll check into a well-appointed room with a king bed, a sofa sleating area, and a bathroom that doesn't make you feel like you're in a budget motel. Hyatt House properties (also frequently Category 1 or 2) often include a complimentary hot breakfast — eggs, waffles, fruit — served every morning. In some suburban markets, these properties also offer free parking, turning your 5,000-point night into an even stronger value play when you factor in parking rates that might otherwise run $20–$30/night.

This isn't a flashy Park Hyatt penthouse suite. But it's a genuinely comfortable, predictably high-quality stay that you've effectively taken off your cash budget — freeing that $338 for experiences, food, or your investment accounts. That's the ChooseFI mindset applied to travel.

Stack your Hyatt Globalist benefits if you qualify. If you hold World of Hyatt's top elite status (Globalist, earned at 60 qualifying nights), you receive complimentary breakfast at most full-service properties and room upgrades. Even on a 5,000-point award night, your elite benefits apply. That free breakfast alone can add $25–$35 of value to every morning.

Use the Hyatt free night award from the World of Hyatt Credit Card. The World of Hyatt Credit Card (issued by Chase) comes with an annual free night certificate valid at Category 1–4 properties. Stack this with a paid or points night to effectively get one night free on a multi-night stay — no points required.

Book as far out as you can. The Hyatt booking window opens 395 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer weekends, holiday weekends, major events — inventory at Category 1 properties can thin out. Getting in early locks your room and your rate.

Target Hyatt House properties for family trips. Hyatt House locations frequently feature suite-style rooms with full kitchens, separate living areas, and free hot breakfast included for all guests. A family of four can stay comfortably for 5,000–8,000 points and skip the cost of restaurant breakfasts entirely.

Earn points on the Bilt card on Rent Day. Bilt Rewards runs a bonus promotion on the first of each month — transferring points earned that day at elevated rates. Accumulating Bilt points through rent payments (no transaction fee) is one of the most efficient ways to build a Hyatt balance.

Don't transfer points speculatively. Even though Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant, always confirm your specific dates show award availability before transferring. Points transferred to Hyatt cannot be moved back.

Don't ignore the expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. A single qualifying activity — a points transfer, a stay, a credit card purchase — resets the clock. Set a calendar reminder annually to ensure you don't lose your balance.

Don't overlook Category 2 properties. At 8,000 points per night, Category 2 Hyatts often include urban full-service hotels that provide dramatically more value than the jump in points cost suggests. Once you're comfortable with Category 1 redemptions, explore Category 2 as a natural next step.

This redemption was built for the travel rewards beginner — the person who has accumulated their first 10,000–20,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt points and isn't yet sure if the whole system is real. It's also for the seasoned optimizer who wants a reliable, low-friction redemption they can execute on short notice.

Minimum points needed: 5,000 for a single night. Most people engaging seriously with Chase UR earning will accumulate this through normal spending in a single billing cycle.

In the broader ChooseFI travel strategy, Category 1 Hyatt nights serve as the building blocks — the reliable, repeatable foundation that funds your domestic travel while you accumulate larger balances for the aspirational redemptions.

**Difficulty Rating: Easy — and we mean it.** This is the redemption we'd hand to someone who just got their first travel rewards credit card and wants to see if the points are real. The score of 5/5 on Beginner Friendliness reflects every dimension of the experience: earning the points is straightforward, the transfer path is clear, the booking interface is clean, and availability is abundant. **What makes this easy:** - **No complex routing rules.** There's no geographic zone logic, no partner airline ticketing, no stopover rules to navigate. You pick a hotel, check availability, transfer points, and book. That's the entire process. - **Instant transfers.** Both Chase Ultimate Rewards and Bilt Rewards transfer to World of Hyatt instantly. You can go from zero Hyatt points to a confirmed reservation in under five minutes. - **Reliable availability.** Category 1 properties are upper-midscale hotels with large room inventories. Award availability is rarely the bottleneck at this tier. **The one thing to watch:** Points don't live in Hyatt until you transfer them — and they can't come back once transferred. Always search hyatt.com *first*, confirm your dates show award space, *then* transfer. This single habit eliminates the only real risk in the process. **Tips for first-timers:** 1. Create your free World of Hyatt account before you need it — having your membership number ready speeds the transfer process. 2. Start with a one-night stay to build confidence, then scale up. 3. Screenshot your confirmation email and points balance after booking — it feels good, and it's good record-keeping. If you've ever booked a hotel room online, you can execute this redemption. Go do it.

Category 1 primarily includes Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties in secondary markets, smaller cities, and suburban locations. These are upper-midscale hotels with consistently good quality — clean rooms, modern decor, and amenities like free Wi-Fi. Hyatt House properties often include complimentary breakfast and kitchen suites.

You need a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred to access transfer partners. The Chase Freedom Unlimited and Freedom Flex can pool points into a Sapphire account for transfers.

However, award availability itself can vary — popular properties during high-demand weekends may show no award availability even though the price remains 5,000 points when rooms are available.

At 5,000 points for a $100 to $200 room, you are getting 2 to 4 cents per point — two to four times the value of redeeming the same Chase Ultimate Rewards points as 1 cent per point cash back. Even compared to the Sapphire Reserve portal rate of 1.5 cents per point, Category 1 Hyatt bookings consistently deliver superior value. Note that Sapphire Preferred holders transfer at 4:3, so factor in the conversion when comparing.

Category 1 Hyatt hotels are the single best entry point into travel rewards for the FI community. At 5,000 points per night with cash values of $100 to $200, you consistently achieve 2 to 4 cents per point — a redemption rate that proves the system works before you ever attempt a complex international booking. Transfer points instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards (1:1 via Sapphire Reserve, 4:3 via Sapphire Preferred) or Bilt (1:1), book directly through Hyatt, and pay only taxes at checkout. This is the foundational redemption that builds your travel rewards confidence and conviction.

#9017. The Best Tri Suits for Postpartum Bodies (That Actually Offer Support)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Gearing up for your first triathlon postpartum, you’ve certainly got a lot on your mind. Most of it probably has nothing to do with you. Who will take care of your child for so many hours? What will they eat? Are they going to miss nap time? Still, you’ll need to make sure that you have all the right equipment and fuel laid out the night before the race.

And while there might not be a “postpartum” filter on triathlon brands’ websites, it’s worth looking into purchasing a new tri suit to accommodate and support the same evolving body that has nourished both you and baby over the past few years.

If you’re still lactating and plan on expressing milk during the race, finding a tri kit with good access is especially crucial. Many mothers have publicly pumped milk while racing (if you’re thinking of doing the same, read my tips for why (and how) new moms should breastfeed during a triathlon).

One common refrain among lactating athletes is that we need more appropriate gear to better facilitate mid-race expression. In testing these tri suits, I therefore paid special attention to how easy each one was to unzip and slip a breast pump inside. That usually hinged on how deep a suit’s zipper was and if it had sleeves. Of course, it also helps to have a nursing sports bra underneath. And because you may be required to carry a hand pump the entire length of a race, I also noted whether pockets were spacious enough to accommodate such equipment.

Not every mother expresses milk, however. That’s why I examined several other aspects of these suits that specifically impact postpartum bodies. For starters, compression. At 2 ½ years postpartum, my body still doesn’t look like it did before baby, and compression in a tri suit can aid in keeping everything from feeling “loose.” However, if you find tight suits restrictive to your airways or range of motion, you might look for the suits with fewer stars in that category.

I also focused on how easy it is to pull each suit down for bathroom breaks (sorry, coach, but there’s gonna be more of them in motherhood). And while chafing is always a concern among triathletes, you might find yourself chafing more and/or in different places as your body fat redistributes itself postpartum. Of course, in addition to all these factors, I rated suits according to more traditional criteria like durability and fit.

Again, don’t simply go for the suit with the most stars. Consider your unique needs, and try suits on before ripping off the tags in excitement. This article is meant to offer helpful insights as you return to racing postpartum, but as you know by now, every mom’s journey is different. What matters most is that you return to the start line on your own time and in your own style.

Size options: XXS, XS, S, M, L, XL Styles: Sleeveless, Sleeved, Tank, Shorts

If you’re just getting back into racing postpartum, a sprint triathlon may be first on your agenda. There are suits designed for that, including the 2XU Core Tri Suit. I wouldn’t wear this for a half or full Ironman — there aren’t enough pockets to store nutrition, and while the padding is high-quality, it’s also minimal. But it’s an excellent option for shorter races, as long as you’re fine with a looser fit. Plus, this suit is relatively easy on the wallet, which can come as a blessing since child-rearing is financially difficult enough.

Former competitive swimmers will understand me when I say this suit is more like an Aquablade than a Fastskin in terms of compression. Some postpartum women will appreciate the looser belly fit, as well as the fact that this suit will accommodate some amount of weight fluctuation and body recomposition as you get back into racing. Even so, the extra folds of fabric did nothing to help the already subpar breathability of this suit. The midriff trapped heat and sweat more than any other suit I’ve ever worn. I was asked to determine if any of these suits were “swamp-assy,” and this one certainly leaned that way. Still, I loved how the open back made me feel like I wasn’t wearing anything at all on my shoulders.

For those concerned about lactation, the zipper of this suit didn’t zip down far enough to accommodate easy breastfeeding or pumping. For shorter distances, though, that’s likely not an issue. The top of the zipper reached unusually high, touching the base of my neck, and it chafed me slightly on the run. Finally, a few loose threads along the seams concerned me about how this suit would hold up across more than one racing season.

Size options: XS, S, M, L, XL, 2XL Styles: Sleeved, Sleeveless, Jersey, Shorts

I wanted to like this suit so that I could rock its floral design at my next Ironman, but I had to knock off several stars because of the terrible chafing it caused in my armpits. That’s not a problem I usually experience, even with sleeved tri suits, but I couldn’t even finish a 3-mile run without my skin screaming in pain. I even felt the suit chafing me while swimming.

It seems I’m not alone, either; I recently spoke to someone else who has suffered unusual chafing in the armpits from a Zoot suit. Nevertheless, there are plenty of folks who peel off this suit after a race and find themselves untarnished, so it’s worth trying on for size (or simply opting for the sleeveless version). Keep in mind that if you’re recently postpartum and had a C-section, the high waistline might irritate the scar.

What I most loved about this suit (aside from its aesthetics) was its full frontal zipper, making dressing and undressing a breeze. My breasts aren’t small, and yet, I had no difficulty cajoling the zipper up or down. Furthermore, you could easily let the top portion of this suit hang loose while breastfeeding a baby. I also appreciated the numerous pockets, though they weren’t very spacious. The cooling pockets, found on the neck and kidney area, were the cherry on top of what was already great breathability.

Size options: XS, S, M, L, XL, 2XL, 3XL Styles: Sleeved, Sleeveless, Sleeved top, Tank top, Shorts

This suit struck the perfect balance between price and performance, and it especially stood out for its medium-high, yet comfortable, level of compression. Because it’s sleeveless and features a full frontal zipper, it’s relatively easy to pull on and take off – whether that’s to pump milk or to hit the restroom. Still, the upper-body compression meant that the zipper was a little harder to tug up over a larger breast size. Plus, the top of the zipper chafed me slightly while running – the protective flap should have been larger.

If you’ve ever complained about how minuscule girl pockets are, this suit will please you with its two large hip pockets, each of which could fit an item as large as a handheld breast pump (or extra chamois butter if you find yourself chafing more postpartum). Those are in addition to two smaller, though still relatively sizable, pockets on the back.

For the most part, this is a great option if you feel like elite suits restrict your airways or range of motion. It performed spectacularly in the water due to its flexibility and sleeveless nature. I also loved how securely the grippers glued the shorts portion to my legs so that they never rode up. Even so, this suit felt slightly tight across my back as I cycled, especially because I hunch slightly more than is good for me.

Size options: XS, S, ST, M, MT, L, LT, XL Available styles: Short sleeve, Sleeveless, Short sleeve tri top, Sleeveless tri top, Tri shorts

This suit fit so snugly and comfortably that I had difficulty finding anything to criticize. I typically don’t love sleeved suits, but the thin, breathable fabric on this one made me forget that I was going rogue. It’s high on the compression factor, which is ideal if you want more core support and to shave off every second possible from your time. Still, the sleeves were flexible and loose enough to allow full range of motion.

Did I wish that this suit came in something other than black or black-and-white? Yes. Not only because a bit of brightness cheers me up when I feel like puking on the run course, but also because my personal cheerleading squad can spot me from a greater distance when I’m wearing bright colors. Still, they say black is classy, so I’m willing to hang up my dreams of a tie-dye race suit for a little while longer. That said, I did notice a bit of color leaking out of the suit once while handwashing it.

The full frontal zipper will be easy to negotiate for those with smaller breasts, but if yours are naturally larger or engorged from breastfeeding, be prepared to possibly spend a few extra seconds aligning and jostling it up. Finally, you won’t be able to overpack with this suit; the two back pockets are medium at best and diagonally aligned.
