#9011. The Best Triathlon GPS Smartwatches of 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

How we reported this: Editor-in-chief Chris Foster has spent hundreds of hours using these watches for training, everyday wear, and nighttime metrics. Foster has independently tested nearly every smartwatch/GPS watch that’s been released in the last eight years, and draws on a decade of making a living as a pro triathlete to inform his impressions. The brands provide all watches on loan.

If you’re a triathlete in the market for a smartwatch or GPS watch, the options just keep getting better. Some of the best triathlon watches in 2026 are getting cheaper, and high-end features that used to cost over $800 are coming down into the $400 range.

What is the only differentiator between a good GPS watch for triathletes and a great one in 2026? It boils down to which is easiest to use, which has those sneaky features you didn’t know you needed, and what you’re (actually) going to do with it.

Below we’ve got brand-new, editor-tested smartwatches and GPS watches from Suunto, Apple, Coros, Amazfit, and Garmin that have all been released in fall 2026. Our editors spend hours training and sleeping with these watches to see what works as advertised, what provides the most accurate (and useful) information, and if it’s intuitive or not.

We review these through the lens of a triathlete who trains multiple times per week, wants to know how their body is reacting to their training, and relies on the data and information for important training and racing decisions. Read on for our expert impressions.

We’ve also included a “Where does it stand?” section for each watch to help you understand where it fits in today’s smartwatch universe. And if you want to dig deeper, we’ve got links to longer reviews for most of the watches below.

Looking for an older smartwatch? We don’t miss much, so check out our previous roundups for quick looks and deep dives on watches from previous years, like the Garmin Fenix 8 or the Suunto Race S – take a look at the 2024 roundup for more.

We’ve also got watches from 2023, like the Polar Pacer, Coros Apex 2 Pro, Garmin Forerunner 965, Suunto 9 Peak Pro, Apple Watch Ultra 1, and Garmin Enduro 2. Or watches from 2022, like the Timex R300, Wahoo Rival, Apple Watch Series 7, Garmin Instinct 2 Solar, Polar Grit X Pro, Suunto 9 Peak, Coros Vertix 2, and Garmin Fenix 7X Solar. Or our 2020 buyer’s guide with reviews of the Coros Pace 2, Apple Watch SE, Garmin Forerunner 745, Fitbit Sense, Polar Vantage V2, and Suunto 7.

The Suunto Race 3S is the little cousin of a slightly larger (but cheaper) Race 2. The Race 3S has a 1.32-inch AMOLED touchscreen that maxes out at 2,000 nits, with 45 hours of multi-band GPS and 64GB of offline mapping and music storage. Like the Race 2, it has sapphire crystal glass, but unlike the Race 2, it weighs in at around 56g compared to the Race 2’s beefy 76g.

The specs are pretty much what you’d expect for a watch in the $400-600 price range, and in real-life testing, the Race 3S also felt nearly identical to the brand-new $400 Suunto Run 2, which was just released about a month ago: They look nearly the same, they feel, weigh, and perform pretty much exactly the same, but the Run 2 only has 24 hours of multi-band GPS and 10 days of advertised daily use (though we found less than that, closer to right days). That said, the Run 2 is $200 cheaper than the Race 3S, so you’re basically paying $200 for a little more battery life, but materially not much else.

While the Race 3S is a fine smartwatch out of context, once you put it up against other smartwatches in the $400-600 range, it struggles a little bit to find its place. First, the elephant in the room is that the Suunto Race 2 has more battery life (and a bigger screen, for better or for worse) for less money. In some ways, the Race 3S is more like a Race 2S, especially given that it’s almost unfair to compare the Race 3S to the original Race S that was released two years ago. But even then, if this was a Race 2S (which it’s not), you’d really have to want a slightly smaller watch to spend less money on an arguably better watch in the Race 2.

The next problem for the Race 3S is also competition from the $400 Run 2, which still isn’t my favorite watch of the year, simply because of the biggest issue Suunto has here: the presence of the $450 Coros Pace 4 Pro. The Pace 4 Pro costs (way) less than the Race 3S, has a bigger screen, weighs slightly less, and has about the same battery life.

The other competition in this price range – watches like the Garmin Forerunner 570 ($550) or the $500 Polar Vantage M3 don’t really overpower the Race 3S, but they’re also not obviously a worse choice. That said, if you put the Race 3S up against Suunto’s own $600 Vertical 2 – with much more battery life, a bigger screen, and an awesome LED flashlight, it’s not even a fair fight. I’d easily spend another $100 for that watch, but it’s the same price.

That said, I’m not sure exactly who the Suunto Race 3S is for. It faces stiff competition from older Suunto watches, like the Race 2 or the Vertical 2, and it struggles mightily against watches like the Coros Pace 4 Pro, or even the $250 Coros Pace 4 (if size/weight truly is your goal and you really need a smaller, ultra-lightweight watch with just enough features and onboard mapping).

The Coros Pace 4 Pro is the latest in one of my favorite lines of endurance-focused smartwatches. Beginning with the almost-too-cheap Pace 2, Coros has taken chunks out of the smartwatch market with a super lightweight and entirely capable offering that doesn’t break the bank. Released less than a year ago, the Pace 4 was arguably one of the best smartwatches for the money, and it was hard to imagine what could come next.

But here we are with the Pace 4 Pro, boasting a big, bright 37.3mm screen with a blinding 3,500nits. This is a big deal because in bright sunlight, if you’re actually using the 32GB of onboard navigation, you need a big screen to see it all, and it needs to be bright enough to see in direct sunlight. Pair those features with the digital dial (essential for zooming navigation on the go, in my opinion), and you’ve already got a best-in-class watch for routing and mapping. All for $450.

Past that, at 51g plus a super-thin side profile, the Pace 4 Pro disappears on one’s wrist in a way that very few watches with these features do. For those of us with small wrists (or those of us who struggle to remove a wetsuit quickly over their watch), this is a big deal.

If there’s room to complain, the only caveat with the Pace 4 Pro is that the styling is still extremely sporty, and the design doesn’t really lend itself to all-day wear. The titanium case and sapphire glass do help with durability, but I still maintain that the aesthetic isn’t quite there on the mid-to-lower end of the Coros line.

All in all, the Coros Pace 4 Pro is a strong contender for the best watch of the year, especially in the highly competitive $400-600 price range (more on that below), and you’d have a hard time feeling limited with this watch.

First it’s worth noting that the $400-600 price range is by far the most competitive in sport-focused smartwatches. For $450 you can get pretty much everything you used to find on a $1,000 watch — and in many cases these less-expensive models are better than the top of the pile just a few years ago.

The $450 Coros Pace 4 Pro most squarely competes with the Garmin Forerunner 570 ($550), the Polar Vantage M3 ($500), the Coros Apex 2 ($480), the Suunto Race 2 ($500), and the Suunto Vertical 2 ($600). You could also include the new Suunto Run 2 ($350), but I don’t think that’s a fair fight.

To my mind, only the Suunto Race 2 and the Suunto Vertical 2 truly compete because the Forerunner 570 costs more and has way less battery (and a smaller screen), the Polar has a host of issues, and the Apex 2’s screen isn’t even in the same league as the Pace 4 Pro.

When squared up against the Suunto Race 2, you’re spending $50 more for a watch with slightly worse battery life, a similarly sized screen (though not as bright as the Pace 4 Pro), but arguably better styling. The Race 2 is also heavier (by a bit) and bulkier.

When up against the Vertical 2, the Suunto easily wins on battery life and the not-to-be-ignored LED flashlight (early morning transitions anyone?) with a similarly sized screen, but it’s a chunker to be sure and costs $100 more — it also lacks a digital dial, which hurts its nav use more than you’d think.

To me, it’s a toss-up between the three, but if money is an object and style is not, the fantastic Coros Pace 4 Pro is the winner.

When the first Apple Watch Ultra was released back in 2022, the big tagline (for triathletes, anyway) was: The First Apple Watch That Can Do An Ironman. It was notable because Apple’s previous smartwatches were so heavy on lifestyle features and light on battery power that you literally couldn’t complete a 10-15-hour Ironman wearing one — even if you felt the sports features were robust enough to be helpful, which they weren’t at the time.

In the years since, Apple has consistently produced one of the prettiest, brightest, fastest, and most feature-packed smartwatches for 80% of the population, but even the Ultra line struggled to stand out — especially as the Ultra line made minor changes from version to version: The Ultra 2 brightened the screen, which was nice; the 3 added satellite emergency SOS and a sweeter screen, but almost nothing else. To the latter upgrades, I still maintain that relying on any smartwatch for SOS/satellite comms in the backcountry over a dedicated device like an inReach or even your phone is a very narrow use case and feels extremely reckless, but that’s just me.

But now enter the Ultra 4, which in my opinion is the most relevant upgrade for triathletes since the first version leapt above the Watch Series line. The Ultra 4 has all of the above upgrades but adds some of the most sensitive and accurate heart-rate sensing/physio tracking that I’ve ever used (this is good news for triathletes).

After testing a load of smartwatches this year with sleep tracking that ranges from “good enough” to “seriously I’ve been awake for hours,” only the Ultra 4’s “Overnight Vitals” syncs up with my true sleep cycles and accurately flagged a bad infection that was developing in my leg. I wasn’t even experiencing fever or any outward effects, but the thoughtful (and easy-to-use) combination of very accurate heart rate, accurate sleep cycles, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and HRV detected the rise and fall of the infection.

I was similarly impressed with the readiness app that helped guide my activity based on vitals and previous activities. Sure, almost every other endurance-focused smartwatch has these features, but none are as accurate and easy to digest.

The last note may seem minor, but it’s not: With the slight increase in battery life, you can now make it through two sleeps before recharging, which means you’re less likely to have to charge overnight or miss/delay a workout while it charges. Yes, 2-3 days is still like 1/8th of most endurance-focused smartwatches, but giving yourself two nights (and a speedier charger that gives you 18 hours in only 15 minutes), it’s finally usable for daily multisport wear and training.

So when you look at the $800-$1,000 price range, you’re looking at smartwatches that do everything and last forever. Up against the $1,000 Garmin Fenix 9, for instance, you’ve got satellite/SOS comms (like the Ultra 4), an AMOLED touchscreen, and pretty much everything else a smartwatch can do — including things like offline voice commands, hands-free calling, an LED flashlight, and more. Most crucially, you’re also getting two weeks or more of battery life to the Ultra 4’s 2-3 days.

That said, if you’re an iPhone user, there is a host of connectivity and lifestyle features that are truly enhanced by the Ultra 4. You can respond to texts, Slacks, sync up everyday mapping and navigation (like when you’re driving around), and way more. No Garmin device (or any other brand) does that with Apple smartphones.

However, if you’re an Android user, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is wildly overpriced and underpowered because it won’t connect at all with your device (Garmin et al. will). Looking down into the super-competitive $600-ish price range, I’d recommend buyers strongly compare the Ultra 4 to the $600 Suunto Vertical 2 thanks to its LED flashlight and exceptional mapping and battery life. I’d also consider the way overfeatured (almost to a fault) and battery-heavy $650 Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar.

Ever since I noticed 2025 UTMB race winner Ruth Croft’s Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro on her wrist a year ago in Chamonix, France, my interest in China-based Amazfit was rekindled. I did a handful of tests on their early endurance-focused efforts, and I felt them to be so beta that I passed on reviewing their models for a few years. Since the T-Rex 3 Pro, however, I’ve kept my eyes peeled for another model that might be interesting for triathletes.

The T-Rex Dual Solar certainly met those standards, with a built-in LED flashlight (think: early morning transition areas or dawn/dusk patrol runs), a surprisingly fast AMOLED (and very bright) screen, enough battery life to get past my magic two-week benchmark, and an almost-ludicrous amount of features, on the same level as a Garmin Fenix, but for at least 30% less money.

First, let’s talk about the most obvious feature on this watch: the dual-sided solar panels. Yes, it seems goofy to have solar panels on the back of the watch, but there are absolutely situations where you might want to try to top up (or at least drain slower) your battery life. I would say in backpacking, this use case comes up pretty often. In triathlon training/life, probably less so: If you’re taking off your watch, you might as well charge the thing, which is infinitely faster than even the best wrist-top solar panels. That said, it is a neat little gimmick.

More importantly, the T-Rex Dual Solar is $150 more than the surprisingly capable T-Rex 3 Pro, but the former doesn’t have a ton more than the latter. Both have two-week-ish battery life, a speaker and microphone, an LED flashlight, rugged styling/durability, and a nearly nauseating host of features — of which a handful are materially useful.

We’re in a time when very few watches do much more than others — with the exception of LED flashlights (which I think are super helpful for triathletes), voice inputting (a mic), and onboard satellite/SOS comms (which I think aren’t that helpful). The T-Rex Dual Solar does everything in that list, except the last, which I don’t find much of a use case for. So then you have to ask, does it do all of those things well? And, are those things easy to use? In the case of the T-Rex Dual Solar, the answer is kind of. User interface and bus were always a little bit of a problem with the first run of Amazfit watches, and while this round is way better, they’re still not as intuitive as a Garmin, Coros, or Apple — the three major competitors.

All that said, if you love a bottomless hole of features, strong battery, LED flashlight, and voice features/functions but don’t want to spend more than $700 and don’t care about a hefty weight and giant wrist footprint, this is it — unless of course you’re good with the T-Rex 3 Pro.

In the $600-plus price range, which I consider the premium range of smartwatches, there’s some pretty tough competition for the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar. First, you have the $800 Apple Watch Ultra 4, which gets blown out of the water by the battery life on the T-Rex Solar (and has no LED flashlight), but crushes the Amazfit when it comes to usability and lifestyle features (though irrelevant if you don’t own an iPhone). The latest Ultra also crushes the T-Rex Dual Solar in terms of 24/7 health metrics and physio measuring/monitoring accuracy; the Ultra 4 also has that standalone satellite/SOS comms, and the Amazfit definitely does not.

Above that, the Garmin Fenix 9 comes in around $1,000 and has pretty much everything that the Ultra 4 does, plus an LED flashlight and enough battery life to put up a fight against the T-Rex Dual Solar (though the Garmin would still lose). The Garmin, however, is far more intuitive and easy to use than the Amazfit, and its host of excellent apps (like Spotify, for instance) make it a clear winner. For a Garmin closer in price, the $750 Forerunner 970 also mirrors the T-Rex Dual Solar’s capabilities with easier interfaces (but less battery).

Looking below that, the $400-600 range is also pretty dangerous — especially Amazfit’s own fully capable $400 Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro that’s virtually identical to the T-Rex Dual Solar if you’re not making lots of use of the backside solar panel. Other than that, there are super capable LED flashlight-equipped watches like the Suunto Vertical 2 ($600) that offer much easier-to-use functions with better companion apps.

There was a time when the Garmin Fenix was pricey, but not out of reach. Less than five years ago you could find a brand-new Fenix 7 for $700. The battery would last close to forever, and there was a chance you’d never use half of the features packed into it. For another $100 or so you could get that all-valuable LED flashlight that used to be unique to the line, but now exists on less-expensive Garmin Instincts, the Suunto Vertical 2, and a few models from Amazfit. You’d get a lot for under $1,000, but you’d still probably not use close to all of it.

Fast forward to today, and the least-expensive Fenix 9 is $1,000. Garmin has added an AMOLED screen to some (and significantly lessened battery life on those models), a speaker/mic, faster map processing, and inReach comm options. If you’re really trying to do an apples-to-apples comparison, the 2022 Fenix 7X Pro Solar ($900 when released) and the 2026 Fenix 9 Pro Solar ($1,300) both have MIP screens and big battery life, but the latter has a mic/speaker (and all that comes with it, like voice control), inReach capabilities built in, and more storage/faster processing. With that in mind (and with the added $8/mo+ cost of the inReach plan), triathletes need to be very thoughtful about how they’re actually going to use the Fenix 9.

Since the inReach capabilities are the newest, shiniest thing across the full Fenix 9 line (and the subscription cost isn’t nothing), triathletes need to think about how often they’d go into an off-grid situation without a smartphone — or actual inReach. If you’re venturing into the rugged backcountry for days on end, you should really arm yourself with a dedicated inReach device, like the $300 Messenger. If you’re not going out for multiple days, most Apple phones now have similar sat features. Barring that, do you really need a no-phone, no-inReach device smartwatch? Probably not.

InReach notwithstanding, the Fenix 9 series feels less novel than it used to be for much more than it used to cost; in the context of the mish-mash featured Fenix 8 line — that had inReach functionality on some models, super-bright MicroLED on others — it feels a little redundant. Of course it has a styling, durability, and construction that Fenix fans will naturally gravitate toward, but at over $1,000 it’s becoming a smaller club than it was.

If we’re looking solely at the MIP-screened (meaning not AMOLED, to be clear) solar version Fenix 9 Pro Solar that costs $1,300, you’re in rare air. None of the Fenix 8s (which are nearly identical to the rest of the Fenix 9 series in many ways) have an MIP screen, so you have to go up against some of the (discounted to under $800) Fenix 7Xs that don’t have inReach. In other brands, you’d be talking about the super long-in-the-tooth $600 Coros Vertix 2 with MIP and a bananas amount of battery, but no LED flashlight or inReach, but an arguably better digital dial for offline mapping use.

The only other watch that’s worth mentioning here is the $800 Apple Watch Ultra 4 that interestingly has onboard SOS/satellite capabilities but also a highly advanced AMOLED touchscreen and nearly incomparable battery life. Even if you look at the AMOLED versions of the Fenix 9 Series that start at $1,000, the Garmins are still blowing the doors off the battery life of the Ultra 4; the Apple claps back with vastly superior lifestyle features (for iPhone users) and a mic/speaker.

All that said, if you can live without inReach (like 99.9% of triathletes can) and a mic/speaker isn’t meaningful to you, now you’re looking at watches for easily half the price, making the whole value proposition pretty tough to stomach. Even the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar mentioned here adds a (not-as-good) mic/speaker and has an LED flashlight for $650.

*Tri Battery Life includes the following settings/uses: Always-on display with the lowest possible brightness for bright daylight use; sleep and all-day heart-rate tracking; HRV tracking; 1-2 workouts/day with max GPS accuracy.

#9010. How to Start a Workout When You Really Don’t Feel Like It (The Bridge Task Method)

If you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself. It’s the gear shift from “couch” to “go.”

A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.

Below is the 5-step version one of our coaching clients uses with her own students, plus a free worksheet to map your own.

A few weeks ago I was talking with Tabitha, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, about a challenge a lot of people face. ​ Some quick context: Tabitha is an executive function coach. She helps neurodivergent students and their families build the skills and systems that support their academic and personal goals. ​ And she noticed something: ​ The challenge of getting started on a workout is almost identical to the challenge her students face when trying to start homework. ​ This might sound familiar. You get home after a long day, mentally fried, and all you want to do is veg out on the couch. ​ In that state, getting up to cook a healthy dinner or go do a workout can feel really freaking hard.

Switching from a “YEAH!” task (chilling on the couch) to a “NAH!” task (workout/homework), is often harder than the task itself.

If we can make that gear shift less dramatic, it can make a big difference!

Instead of going from YEAH! to NAH!, you insert at least one task that’s just…MEH.

If you’re struggling to start your workout, don’t fight the gear change. Bridge it.

Add a little MEH to the mix and see what happens.

Tabitha put together a free worksheet that walks you through mapping your own task initiation sequence. Your personal YEAH -> MEH -> NAH.

Try it this week, and keep me posted on how it goes. ​ You got this. ​ -Matt

#9009. Over a Tenth of Your Clients Are Dealing With IBS—And Here’s How to Help

This is according to the results of a study of nearly 2,000 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).1

In other research, people with IBS said they would take a medicine that carried a one percent risk of sudden death if it would cure their symptoms2—which can include urgent bouts of diarrhea, gas, or persistent constipation.

Some people with IBS experience bouts of abdominal pain they describe as worse than childbirth. These flare-ups can siphon concentration, interrupt sleep, and destroy work productivity.3

As a result, many people with IBS plan their lives around the availability of private, clean bathrooms. Fear of a sudden flare-up leads some to avoid restaurants, get-togethers, even exercising in public.

This pervading worry has a name—gastrointestinal-specific anxiety—and it can affect everything from social relationships to overall well-being. It’s also the main reason people with IBS report worse quality of life than people with other chronic conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, and end-stage kidney disease.4

PN Super Coach Sarah Maughan, certified through Monash University—a global leader in understanding the link between food sensitivities and IBS—has witnessed how lifestyle changes can prevent flare-ups, calm GI anxiety, and allow people with IBS to live the lives they want.

“My hope is for everyone with IBS to know they have options, whether that’s turning to a physician for medication and/or a health coach to learn about lifestyle changes and how to put them into action,” says Maughan.

In this article, we’ll hear more from Maughan. You’ll also learn:

Plus, if you’re a health coach, you’ll learn how to support clients with IBS while safely staying within your scope of practice.

Sometimes referred to as “spastic colon,” IBS is the most commonly diagnosed digestive disorder in the world, affecting about 14 percent percent of adults.5

Unlike Crohn’s and other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), IBS doesn’t alter the architecture of the gut. When healthcare professionals use diagnostic imaging, they find no infections, inflammation, damage to the bowel wall, or other evidence of disease.

Years ago, this lack of visible disease led many healthcare professionals to assume that IBS was purely psychological. More recently, however, this thinking has shifted.

Experts now view IBS as a functional neuro-gastrointestinal disorder.

That means the nerves between the GI tract and the brain don’t function optimally, causing the brain to deliver unnecessary pain signals and interfere with typical bowel function.

IBS symptoms can come and go, with some people experiencing months or years of relief only to suffer a severe flare-up that can last hours to weeks.

In addition, not everyone with IBS experiences the same set of symptoms, which can make the condition challenging to diagnose.

The below illustration shows the range of IBS symptoms.

Researchers are still trying to understand why the gut functions differently in people with IBS. However, they do have a few theories.

According to one hypothesis, the nerve endings in the GI tract may be overly sensitive in people with IBS. This can lead to two different sets of symptoms.

▶ Hypersensitive nerves communicate pain signals to the brain, causing people with IBS to notice digestive processes that other people wouldn’t feel. Tiny gas bubbles may be severely uncomfortable for someone with IBS, for example, but not bother someone without the disorder.

▶ Overreactive nerves can trigger GI muscles to contract with too much force, leading to gas, bloating, and diarrhea. If they underreact, the same muscles don’t contract forcefully enough, which slows the passage of food through the intestine and leads to constipation.

Another theory blames disturbances on the gut microbiome, which helps to explain why some people develop IBS symptoms after first having a severe GI illness like the Norovirus.

If you or your client suspect IBS, see a credentialed health professional.

The symptoms of IBS overlap with several other gastrointestinal diseases and health conditions that can require medication, surgery, or medically-supervised lifestyle changes. These include infections, inflammatory bowel diseases, celiac disease, cancer, and food allergies, among others.

It’s especially important to see a medical professional if you or your client notice any of the following:

In addition to ruling out other GI conditions, a healthcare professional will also ask detailed questions about you or your client’s symptoms. This information allows them to pinpoint which IBS “type” you or your client might have:

You or your client’s IBS type will inform what your healthcare professional recommends.

A healthcare provider might suggest a short course of antibiotics and antidiarrheal medicine for IBS-D. On the other hand, for IBS-C, they might recommend a fiber supplement, non-habit-forming laxative, laxative-like medication, or other medicine that reduces the perception of pain and regulates bowel movements.

In order to get the most out of the visit, you can help your client (or yourself) prepare for a healthcare appointment.

A healthcare professional will likely ask the following questions, so consider the responses beforehand:

Another way to prepare for your first appointment?

Well, you might not like it, but it’s a good idea to…

Consider keeping a poo diary for a couple of weeks before your appointment.

In the diary, track the frequency of bowel movements and other symptoms. Use the Bristol Stool Chart (below) to take note of the quality of your poo. This information can help your healthcare professional assess whether you have IBS and which type.

(To learn more about the clues your poos can hide, read: 6 reasons you should care about your poop health)

In recent years, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved several new prescription medicines for IBS, along with a medical device that stimulates the cranial nerves behind the ear.

In addition, thousands of research papers have looked at the interaction between IBS and various lifestyle habits, with many promising findings.

Here are five evidence-based ways to reduce the symptoms of IBS (and bonus, many of them are great for enhancing overall health too).

People with IBS who exercise regularly tend to experience fewer symptoms and flare-ups than people who don’t exercise.

When researchers asked people with IBS to walk moderately for an hour three times a week, study participants experienced significant relief from bloating and abdominal pain within 12 weeks.6

How exercise soothes IBS isn’t fully understood, though.

According to other research, exercise may reduce stress and improve mental health, which, in turn, may help improve communication between the gut and the brain.7 8

Another theory argues that exercise helps encourage the growth of health-promoting gut bacteria, which may help to break down food more efficiently and decrease inflammation.9

Anxiety, stress, and depression all activate stress hormones like norepinephrine (noradrenaline) and cortisol, which can:

Of course, stress doesn’t come with an on/off switch.

Simply telling yourself, “Stop getting so stressed out!” won’t likely help—and may even paradoxically lead to more stress.

That’s why Precision Nutrition-certified coaches like Maughan help clients learn to focus on what’s within their control—such as practicing self-compassion, or experimenting with nervous system regulators like yoga, breathing exercises, and gentle walking.

As the image below illustrates, clients can control how they perceive, respond to, and anticipate stressors—but not always the stressors themselves.

Either way, when clients focus more on what they can control and less on what they can’t, they often feel calmer and more capable.

(If you want to help a client figure out just what’s within their control—and what’s not—try out our free worksheet: Sphere of Control Worksheet)

(Assess your current stress load by taking our free quiz: Do you have a Stress Bod?)

PN coaches have long appreciated and advocated slower, more relaxed eating.

Yes, slow eating helps people fill up on fewer calories—but it also tends to help clients reduce or even eliminate GI woes like acid reflux, bloating, and pain.

For one, slower eating often translates to more chewing. In addition to mechanically mashing food into a pulp, increased chewing also allows the mouth’s digestive enzymes to pre-digest food. As a result, the stomach and intestines have to work less hard.

Plus, eating in a relaxed setting often lowers stress hormones like norepinephrine and cortisol, making it less likely that they will intensify GI pain signals.

According to Maughan, this can be especially important for young parents, as it’s not always easy to eat undistracted and peacefully when tending to little ones.

(Sounds simple, but slow eating is more challenging than people think—and a lot more impactful. Learn more: Try the slow-eating 30-day challenge.)

According to research, people with IBS experience more shallow, less restorative, and more interrupted sleep.13

Because of poor sleep quality, many people with IBS sleep more hours overall than people without IBS—yet feel less rested.

Fatigue can then set off a vicious cycle. When people don’t sleep restfully, stress hormone levels tend to be higher, which can exacerbate gut pain.14

Unrested people also tend to feel hungrier during the day. Cravings for fats and sweets also intensify, driving people to reach for the very foods more likely to trigger IBS symptoms—and wolf them down too quickly.

As with stress, you can’t simply will yourself to sleep more restfully.

However, the first three strategies—exercise, stress management, and slower eating—can all help.

Some PN clients have found that consuming a smaller dinner earlier in the evening gives their bodies more time to digest before bed. Other clients tell us that a relaxing pre-bedtime routine—a few minutes of foam rolling, a guided meditation, a bath, or some journalling—tends to help.

(Find out the best practices for getting better sleep by checking out our infographic: The power of sleep)

While there’s no one-size-fits-all IBS diet, experts have identified several food categories that are more likely to be problematic for many people. These include:

▶ Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, and Polyols (FODMAPs), which are a family of carbohydrate-rich foods that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine. Even in people without IBS, these foods tend to slow digestion and attract water. When gut bacteria ferment them, they produce gas, which can stretch the intestinal wall. For most, this slowed digestion and gas isn’t especially noticeable; In people with IBS, it can lead to intense pain. High-FODMAP foods include wheat, rye, barley, onions, garlic, beans, dairy, honey, cashews, some processed meats, and many fruits and vegetables. (More about FODMAPs in the next section.)

▶ Caffeinated beverages and foods, especially coffee, which trigger the release of stress hormones, stimulate the production of stomach acid, increase muscle contractions in the colon, and irritate the lining of the intestine.15

▶ Alcohol and spicy foods that irritate the gut.16 17

▶ High fructose corn syrup and sugar alcohols such sorbitol and mannitol, which have been linked to gas, bloating, and diarrhea in susceptible people.18 19

▶ Fatty, greasy foods, which can slow digestion and attract water, leading to loose stools, bloating, and gas.20 21

If the idea of giving up all the foods and beverages on the above list has you in a cold sweat, know this…

Not everyone with IBS is sensitive to the same foods and beverages.

“Everyone can have different triggers,” says Maughan. “That’s why it’s so important to figure out what makes your body feel good and what doesn’t.”

Some people struggle with apples but are okay with berries. Others can drink green tea but not black. One person might be able to consume five to eight ounces of beer but not 12. A gluten-free diet may work great for some but not others.

Similarly, many people find relief by avoiding certain high-FODMAP foods. However, you may only be sensitive to some FODMAPs and not others. If so, eliminating all FODMAPs would be unnecessarily restrictive and difficult to follow consistently.

For this reason, it can be helpful to try an elimination diet to see which foods and beverages are problematic—along with the quantities you can safely tolerate, says Maughan. You’ll learn more about elimination diets in the next section.

(Want someone to walk you through exactly how to do an elimination diet? Read: How and why to do an elimination diet.)

In our online coaching communities, we often see people asking some version of the following question:

“My client just told me that she has IBS. Am I allowed to continue to coach this person?”

As we mentioned, Maughan specializes in helping people with digestive problems. Coaching someone with IBS is no different than coaching a client with any other nutritional goal, she says.

“Because IBS is often largely associated with what someone eats, it’s within a coach’s wheelhouse—with some caveats,” says Maughan. “You can’t diagnose your client with the condition, and you should make it clear that you’re not prescribing a diet for them. In addition, you should encourage clients to seek care from a medical professional, especially if you suspect something other than IBS is going on.”

To stay within your scope of practice, follow these do’s and don’ts.

Elimination diets do what the name suggests: They exclude certain foods for a short period—usually three weeks. Then, you slowly reintroduce specific foods and monitor your symptoms for possible reactions.

Elimination diets work a lot like a science experiment that helps you identify problematic foods.

The phrase “elimination diet” may sound scary and off-putting, as if you’ll be living for months on bland food you have to slurp through a straw.

However, there are many different types of elimination diets, with some much less restrictive than others.

This is an excellent option for people who suspect they already know which foods and beverages trigger symptoms.

It goes like this: You eliminate up to four foods for several weeks. Then, slowly reintroduce them one at a time to see if your symptoms return.

Let’s say, for example, from experience, you know you feel bad whenever you eat dairy. On the lite elimination diet, you’d eliminate just dairy for three weeks. Then you’d reintroduce it to see how you feel.

If you’re unsure of how food interacts with your GI tract—but aren’t ready for a super restrictive eating plan, our Precision Nutrition elimination diet is likely the way to go.

Created by PN and approved by several registered dietitians, the plan removes many of the foods most likely to cause problems, while still including a variety of vegetables, fruits, starches, legumes, nuts, seeds, and meats, so you can continue to eat a well-balanced diet.

To learn more, download our FREE Ultimate Guide to Elimination Diets. This ebook has everything you need to be successful, including an at-a-glance chart that helps you easily follow the diet, along with recipes, meal ideas, and tip sheets.

Over several years, researchers at Monash University in Australia have developed and extensively studied a low-FODMAP elimination diet for people with IBS.22

Unlike other types of elimination diets, the FODMAP diet is a highly specialized form of medical nutrition therapy. The FODMAP diet’s list of problematic foods (shown below) is anything but intuitive, and the reintroduction phase is more complex than other elimination diets.

As a result, if you’ve been diagnosed with IBS and suspect you have a FODMAP issue, seek the expertise of a FODMAP-certified practitioner. You can also download Monash University’s FODMAP Diet app, which will help you navigate low-FODMAP eating.

In isolation, more knowledge doesn’t always lead to more power.

For example, there’s a difference between knowing that dairy messes with your gut and doing something with that knowledge.

Similarly, you might know that you feel better when you eat a small dinner earlier in the evening, but you may struggle to plan your life so an early dinner happens regularly.

This is where a certified health coach can help.

“Many of my clients already have an idea of the foods that tend to cause them problems,” says Maughan, “But they’re nervous to know for sure because they fear that the knowledge will make eating more challenging.”

Even if you do an elimination diet and you learn your favorite food is contributing to your IBS, you don’t have to do anything with that information.

You can choose to continue to eat your favourite foods if you want, AND you can choose to avoid them when it’s really important for you not to experience IBS symptoms, she says.

“With knowledge, you have choices,” says Maughan.

#9008. Does Soreness Mean a Good Workout? No. Here’s What It Actually Tells You

Soreness is not an indicator of a good workout, and not being sore doesn’t mean your workout didn’t count.

That day-after ache (DOMS) mostly tells you that you did something new, not something effective.

Progress is more reliably measured in your training log: more weight, more reps, more control over time, sore or not.

Rachael (a reader and all-around amazing person) sent me a question about this so well-organized it came with multiple choice answers. 😃

I LOVE this question, because almost everyone who’s getting started (or starting again) wonders the same thing:

Quick definition first. That achy, stiff, “why does it hurt to sit on the toilet” feeling that shows up a day or two after a workout has a name: DOMS, or Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness.

It usually peaks somewhere around 24-72 hours after you train.

Severe soreness is NOT an indicator of a good workout.

It’s a sign that you did something new that your body isn’t used to yet:

But it’s also not something to be afraid of, especially if you switch up your routine and are mildly sore for a day or two.

Your body is adapting quickly! And as you adjust to the new exercises, you’ll be less and less sore from it.

So when is soreness helpful, if ever? ​ Soreness can give us a useful signal that we worked a muscle we were trying to target and hadn’t felt before.

But if you’re SUPER sore? Like, can’t get out of bed the next day and have to waddle around like a newborn giraffe sore? That’s a sign the jump was bigger than your body needed.

And the real cost (beyond the discomfort) is that it gets in the way of your next couple of workouts. Either because your technique gets sloppy because everything hurts, or you’re so wrecked that you don’t want to show up at all.

The best way to lower your odds of severe DOMS is to ease into a new program slowly.

Start with fewer sets and lighter weights than you think you need, and build from there. 💪

Yes! You DO need to push yourself over time in order to make progress:

That’s the law of progressive overload, and there’s no getting around it.

Sometimes adding that extra bit will make you sore. Other times, it won’t.

But it’s the underlying principle that matters: are you asking a little more of yourself over time? Not: did it hurt afterward?

So why do we care so much about soreness?

Here’s what I think we’ve fallen into with fitness in general.

We as humans operate really well with feedback. If we touch a hot stove, we get burned and know not to do that again.

We want to know, immediately after doing something, whether it worked or it didn’t.

And with strength training, you don’t feel stronger the next day. It takes time to build up.

So we reach for proxies that close that feedback loop.

It’s exactly like the story of minty toothpaste.

As the story goes, toothpaste manufacturers had a hard time selling their product until they added mint.

Suddenly, there was a tingly clean feeling you could latch onto. “Oh, this IS working.”

The mint doesn’t clean your teeth. But it’s associated with the thing that does, and it gave people something to feel.

It’s not the REASON you’re getting stronger.

But it can be associated with the work you do, especially as a beginner who is new to exercise, so we’ve learned to chase the tingle.

✅ How much weight, how many reps, how many sets are you doing?

✅ Do you feel more stable and controlled with the exercise than you did last month?

Then great! It’s working. Doesn’t matter if you never get sore.

And if you do end up super sore after trying something new, it’s not that you “failed”.

Just take it as a cue to introduce things more gently next time. 😊

So, back to Rachael’s multiple choice question.

C is really close. But I’ll add an fourth option:

D) Soreness tells you what was NEW. Your training log tells you what’s WORKING.

No extra fitness points for being sore. No points off if you do end up sore, either.

All the points gently ramping things up over time, and showing up again next time. 🔥

Is it bad if I’m never sore? No. If your weights, reps, or control are improving over time, your training is working, sore or not.

How long does DOMS last? It usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after the workout and fades over a few days. If you’re regularly wrecked for longer, ease the jumps in your program.

Should I work out while sore? Mild soreness is fine to train through, and easy movement often helps. If you’re severely sore, target a different part of the body, scale down, or take another rest day; what we don’t want to do is have sloppy technique because we’re SO sore we can’t perform the exercise normally.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Humans featured are exceptional examples and do not guarantee individual success. Your experience and results may vary.

#9007. How to Organize an Adaptive Triathlon for Kids (and Why It’ll Change Your Perspective)

Over 25 children participated in the adaptive Kids Tri for Champions event. (Photo: Courtesy Kevin Webb)

For this story, Triathlete spoke with the two organizers of the Kids Tri for Champions and one parent of a participant to understand what it takes to put on an adaptive triathlon for kids.

This whole swim-bike-run experience is supposed to be fun, but chasing PRs and podium finishes can make that easy to forget. If you’re overdue for a reminder, consider helping with an adaptive triathlon for kids.

An adaptive triathlon is not your typical race, and to find out why, as well as learn what it takes to successfully organize one, we spoke with Erik Wanberg, Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine student and the co-founder of Kids Tri for Champions: Adaptive Triathlon, and his co-organizer, Kevin Webb.

In 2024, Wanberg and several other Mayo Clinic medical students founded the first annual Kids Tri for Champions, an adaptive triathlon for children with developmental, intellectual, or physical special needs in grades kindergarten through 12th.

The race was part of the students’ second year of medical school, during which they’re provided with a variety of volunteer opportunities that they can receive school credit for. While they can choose to give back through existing community events and community service, Wanberg and the other students decided to create a new event, bringing their own interest in triathlon to children with disabilities when they realized the sport was inaccessible to them.

Nearly a dozen participants of all ability levels swam, biked, and ran their way to the finish line of the inclusive event at Soldier’s Field Park in Rochester, Minnesota.

“We started this race in an effort to fill an equity gap for children with disabilities in Southern Minnesota,” Wanberg says. “There are excellent resources here for adaptive physical education in our schools and fun after-school activities in our communities, but no real chance for the kids to participate in an actual competition that allows them to have that community race experience.”

Nearly one in five children in Minnesota and 3 million children across the U.S. live with a special health need or impairment. What’s more, physical activity levels are 4.5 times lower for disabled children. And for 1.5 million public primary and secondary school students with a physical disability, athletic competitions remain inaccessible.

“So we set out to create the first adaptive triathlon in this region where kids on the entire spectrum of intellectual and physical disabilities could swim, bike, and run,” Wanberg explains. Rather than emphasize competition, the Kids Tri for Champions focuses on inclusive recreation and self-achievement.

Now in its third year, the triathlon was held on July 11. Webb estimates that over 25 children between the ages of 4 and 18 years old participated.

“Over the past few years, our adaptive triathlon has accommodated children with capabilities ranging from Down syndrome to physical disabilities,” Webb says, “including hearing-impaired athletes and wheelchair users.”

“Adaptive events allow all kids to feel a strong sense of accomplishment,” says Anna Strand, whose daughter Ella is a Kids Tri for Champions’ finisher. “It gives them a chance to connect with friends and to work through a challenge in a way that raises their heart rate and also exposes them to a whole community that is supporting them and cheering them on.”

Inspired to offer an adaptive triathlon for children in your own community? Wanberg and Webb have some invaluable tips for organizing an inclusive event that is fun and safe for kids of all abilities.

1. Do set a date and a rain date, especially if your event will take place during thunderstorm season.

2. Do start planning early. For the Kids Tri for Champions in July, planning usually begins in January or February. Wanberg suggests sending out a Google form/survey that includes a direct question about each participant’s functional/ability level and event needs, including any specific accommodations that they will require during the event, such as an adaptive bike. The form should also include a section where participants can request that an athlete buddy partner with them for the entire race if they don’t want to bring their own. For Kids Tri for Champions, a link to the form is included in a promotional PDF for the event, which sponsors and supporters share on their websites and social media accounts.

3. Do establish a financial support system once you have a sense of how many participants to expect. Webb estimates that the Kids Tri for Champions costs about $400 to $500 annually for finisher medals, shirts, juice, and snacks, most of which is covered by donations from local nonprofits.

4. Do find a pool for the swim and plan your course around that. Kids Tri for Champions books the Soldier’s Field lap pool through Rochester Parks & Recreation, which provides a few lifeguards as well.

5. Do make sure that the course is in a contained environment that is publicly available, legal for the race, and straightforward. Wanberg suggests walking the course you’re considering to ensure there are no bumps, craters, or cracks that might make it hard or unsafe for adaptive bikes or individuals with poor balance.

6. Do put a team of volunteers together. Webb starts by emailing Mayo Clinic medical students.

“We get about 10 medical students, as well as people from the nonprofits We Bike Rochester and EA Therapeutic Health for a total of around 25 volunteers,” Webb says.

7. Do get help borrowing adaptive bikes (which can otherwise be expensive) by building a relationship with a local bike company or non-profit that can help with e-bikes, handcycles, tandems, recumbents, and upright bikes with training wheels. For the Kids Tri for Champions, EA Therapeutic Health brings a trailer of their physical therapy bikes to the race.

8. Do assign a buddy to swim with the athlete and run alongside them while they bike and run if it’s requested in the survey.

“Make sure that a couple of the buddies you recruit can run fast,” Webb advises. “Two years ago, a kid with an electric bike requested a buddy, so I ran with him, but he was doing 5:30 miles! So the next year, I recruited a couple high school cross-country runners just in case we had anyone on a fast bike.”

9. Do be flexible while putting safety first! Some of your participants may not be swimmers, which is why it’s crucial to have lifeguards on duty and floaties available. Have helmets available and insist that every athlete wear one while cycling.

“On race morning, mark the course, put out cones, and position volunteers at key points to keep athletes on the right path, but be ready to let them do their own thing, as long as it’s legal and safe,” Webb says. “One year, we marked the course to go clockwise, but the kid who finished the swim first began biking the other way and that’s what everybody else did. So we went counter-clockwise that day. It’s organized chaos and you have to embrace it.”

1. Don’t charge money. Keep the event free for families to offer a truly accessible triathlon.

2. Don’t limit the event to participants based on their abilities. Tailor the course to children with special needs but realize that part of what makes an adaptive triathlon so memorable for them is the opportunity to participate in an event with their siblings and peers of all abilities.

“This year there were two kids that were just planning on going to the pool that day,” Webb says. “They saw the triathlon and wanted to participate even though they hadn’t signed up, so we let them. That experience exposed them to people who have abilities that are different from their own, which is so cool!”

3. Don’t have a set distance … or order. Start the race in the pool but leave it up to each child to decide how far they feel comfortable swimming, whether that’s one lap or several. When the participant finishes swimming, their buddy can help them transition to the bike.

“In our triathlon, the kids bike on a trail around the pool, and their buddy runs alongside them,” Webb says. “What’s important is that each kid has a buddy with them and can choose for themselves if they want to bike or run a couple laps or turn around.”

4. Don’t underestimate the flexibility needed.

“There will be kids with varying intellectual and physical disabilities,” Wanberg says. “As such, there will be unforeseen obstacles on race day. Be ready to change things on the fly, typically at an individual participant level, if necessary to keep the race safe and fun.”

“We’ve had kids that swim, bike one lap, and jump back in the water instead of running,” Webb says. “Two years ago, I was a buddy for an athlete with Down syndrome who was maybe 10 years old. We were running along the trail and passed a public group doing yoga. He decided that he wanted to join them and the group was cool with it, so we took a yoga break.”

5. Don’t forget how much of an impact an adaptive triathlon can have on the kids – and you!

“Ella ran hard and she was tired, but seeing people cheer for her put a smile on her face,” Strand says. “The most meaningful part was seeing her sense of accomplishment as she finished the race!”

A few years ago, Webb remembers there was a teen at the finish line when he saw his friend starting the run. He just turned around and went with the other kid.

“It’s the opposite of the races I participate in, where it’s all about being competitive,” says Webb, who was part of the University of California, Davis’ Triathlon Club and now competes in trail races. “An adaptive kids triathlon is all about giving these children a sense of belonging in our communities. No matter what their pace or how far they go, I guarantee that they’re having more fun than we do at our races. It’s an awesome reminder to not take being able to run, bike, or swim for granted. It can reframe your perspective on sport.”

#9006. How Fast Do You Actually Lose Strength? Slower Than You Think

You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.

A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).

Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.

Here’s the timeline, and how it can inform your training.

Has this question ever crossed your mind:

This was an awesome question that Charles sent my way. (Thanks Charles! 🙌)

When life gets crazy and you find yourself skipping workouts, there’s a voice that says:

I had that exact thought the first time I had to take significant time away for a back injury.

And heck, just recently my kiddos brought home the “crud” from school and I missed a full week of workouts.

So, let’s look at what actually happens, and what it means for your training.

Short version: a few days off doesn’t impact your maximum strength or muscle size basically at all.

Your muscles may look or feel “flatter”, but that’s because stored water and glycogen decrease, not because you are weaker.

And this “pump” comes back quickly once you start training again. 💪

Here’s a rough timeline of when we start to see the effects of detraining:

Highly trained folks and older adults will notice detraining faster than new or younger lifters (so they’ll sit towards the beginning of these timelines.)

But you don’t lose your progress in any meaningful way after a week or 2 away from the gym. 😊

And if you DO have to spend significant time away for whatever reason, I have good news for you, too:

1) Your nervous system remembers how to do the movement.

The first session or two in the gym after time away may feel a bit clunky, but you’ll quickly regain the technique.

And a big component of strength is neuromuscular coordination (i.e. your brain and muscles firing together more efficiently, which improves rapidly.)

2) The muscle itself seems to hold onto some of the machinery it built, so it rebuilds faster the second time.

A general rule of thumb is about 50% as long as you were away (so if you were away for 12 weeks, it may take ~6 weeks to rebuild your strength.) Take this with a grain of salt as there is a LOT of variation here. This isn’t a hard and fast rule.

(And you don’t want to jump right back in at 100%. Use the 50/50 rule to get yourself going again.)

The point is, it’s generally easier to rebuild than to build the first time.

Building muscle and strength? It takes time and effort.

No one wakes up a day after a workout and has just magically put on 5 pounds of muscle.

That takes only a fraction of the volume.

When you keep intensity the same (i.e. how hard the exercise is), doing 1/3 the number of sets maintains your strength for a loooong time. ​ The point being: doing ANYTHING during a period where you aren’t able to consistently work out is still really really helpful!

When life throws you off track with your fitness goals, you’re not starting back from square zero.

And even a single session each week with a couple challenging sets is enough to hold what you’ve built until things calm down.

There’s that old saying that: “The best time to invest was 20 years ago. The next best time to invest is today.”

I think the same holds true for building up your fitness.

Every session you put in now is strength you get to keep later.

This is exactly why we built our coaching program. Because having a coach makes both of those so much smoother. ​ We take the thinking off your plate so it’s easier to get going.

We direct your limited time and effort toward the stuff that actually moves the needle. ​ AND when life pulls you away (sick kids, a work deadline, etc.) we help you maintain and get right back at it. ​ If that sounds like the kind of help you’ve been looking for, here’s how NF Coaching works. 💪 ​ -Matt

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.
